value: free-living yellowhead wrasse were likely repelled by DMSP in an in situ odorant test on a fringing reef
units: categorical (response statistic, mean of three post-release counts minus the pre-release count, ranked across control, DMSP and betaine tests; two-factor Friedman test, chi-square, df = 2)
method: in situ field odorant-release test on fringing reef at Curacao: a weighted bag of odorant-containing local reef water was ejected remotely and silently over 40 to 50 min (12 to 16 L) into a 4 m x 4 m reef arena with the water column above to about 4 m; each test had six 5-min enumeration periods in which two observers recorded fish species and numbers; response statistic (n2 + n3 + n4)/3 - n0 per species, arena and test; three odorant types (control, DMSP, betaine mix) in random order at each site, the two sites randomised independently; analysed with a two-factor Friedman test with odorant and observer as factors
conditions: wild fish: free-living, non-resident yellowhead wrasse entering and leaving the arenas without evident site fidelity; two sites on the fringing coral reefs of Curacao (Carmabi Buoy 1 and about 0.5 km west near Carmabi Buoy 2), three observation arenas and two odorant release sites per site, bottom depth averaging 9.2 m landward and 10.8 m seaward; 30 June to 13 July 2011; 20 odorant tests in all (6 control, 6 DMSP, 8 betaine mix; control bag filled with plain local seawater); DMSP at 4 x 10^-6 M and betaine mix (glycine betaine, proline betaine, trigonelline) at 2 x 10^-4 M each; yellowhead wrasse abundance index 605 (grand total counted over all 360 enumeration periods); adults and juveniles were summed for this species; Friedman chi-square = 4.95, df = 2, which the paper calls significant only at the p = 0.10 level and not at p = 0.05 ('Although this value is not statistically significant at the p = 0.05 level'); the Results say evidence of a difference among odorants was found only in yellowhead wrasse among the non-resident species analysed, with the response statistic lower in DMSP tests than in control or betaine tests, so no attraction to betaines was found; the Discussion calls this a potential repellent effect; observers were authors, blocked in the Friedman test, and were told odorant identities only after all tests (only RWH knew identities during testing); dye tests showed the ejected water was neutrally buoyant; the paper names sample size as a central challenge ('we found ourselves desiring a database of at least twice the size we obtained') and does not discuss correction for the many species tested; same-paper results for other species (not this value): adult creole wrasse chi-square 5.99 (p = 0.05) repelled by DMSP, adult brown chromis chi-square 4.79 (not significant at 0.05, marginal at 0.10), other species no evidence of an effect

source.authors: Hill RW, Florn AM, Vermeij MJA, Frade PR
source.title: In situ testing of candidate odorant cues in coral-reef fish: a new method with tests of dimethylsulfoniopropionate and betaines

quote: Creole wrasse (Clepticus parrae) and yellowhead wrasse (Halichoeres garnoti) are likely repelled by DMSP.
note: Classification: behavioural_response, change in counts of wild fish in an odorant arena; no chemoreceptor is identified and the cue is a dissolved compound (DMSP). The quote is the whole Abstract sentence; it also names the creole wrasse, which is a separate result not logged here, and the statistics and the p = 0.10 qualifier are carried in conditions. Authority: Catalog of Fishes (researcharchive.calacademy.org fishcatget spid=17104) printed 'Current status: Valid as Halichoeres garnoti (Valenciennes 1839).', family line 'Labridae: Julidinae.'; order Labriformes taken from main. Creole wrasse not filed because the Catalog genus page for Clepticus gives it as a synonym of Bodianus and the spid page found for the species name reads Bodianus parrae.
